v_P(z) = n_P for all P? In other words, we want to prescribe the behavior of the function at all places, what pole and zero orders are concerned. As there are an infinity of places (Corollary 20.18) and z ∈ F has only finitely many poles and zeroes, the answer to the question above can be affirmative only if n_P = 0 for almost all P. It is therefore natural to work with such tuples:

**20.19 Definition.** The divisor group 𝒟_F is the free abelian group generated by the places. We write its elements, the divisors, as A = Σ_P n_P P and also write n_P = v_P(A). The corresponding module is defined as

L(A) = {x ∈ F | v_P(x) + v_P(A) ≥ 0 for all P}.

Further, dim(A) = dim(L(A)) is the dimension of divisor A.

Each divisor prescribes the behavior at each place, and at almost all places it is prescribed that the function be defined at P. The use of the ≥ 0 sign in the definition of the space L(A) weakens the original question. This is motivated by the obvious fact, following from the triangle inequality, that L(A) is a vector space over K.

A divisor D is effective (D ≥ 0) if all its entries are ≥ 0. We write D₁ ≤ D₂ if D₂ − D₁ ≥ 0. Divisors D = 1·P are also called prime divisors. As an example, when is z ∈ L(P)? This means that z is defined at all places ≠ P and z is either defined at P or has a pole there of order at most 1 (v_P(z) ≥ −1). The support of D consists of the places P where v_P(D) ≠ 0. Each divisor D can be written in a unique way as D = D₀ − D_∞, where D₀ (the zero divisor) and D_∞ (the pole divisor) are effective.

**20.20 Definition.** Let x ∈ F. The principal divisor is defined as

(x) = Σ_P v_P(x) P.

Consider also the zero divisor (x)_0 and the pole divisor (x)_∞.

The principal divisors form a subgroup of the divisor group.

**20.21 Definition.** The divisor class group 𝒞_F is the factor group of 𝒟_F mod the group of principal divisors. This defines an equivalence relation on divisors: A ∼ B if these divisors yield the same element of 𝒞_F, equivalently if A − B = (z) is a principal divisor.

We know that the elements of K̃, the constants, are precisely those that do not have zeroes or poles. It follows that L(0) = K̃. As we know that K̃ is a finite-dimensional extension of K, it will not do much harm to assume K̃ = K.

**20.22 Proposition.** L(0) = K, dim(0) = 1, where it is assumed for the remainder of the text that K̃ = K is the full constant field.
